```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import logsumexp

np.random.seed(495)
plt.style.use("ggplot")

def show(df, fmt=None, caption=None):
    sty = df.style.hide(axis="index")
    if fmt:
        sty = sty.format(fmt)
    if caption:
        sty = sty.set_caption(caption)
    return sty
```

## Introduction

When we want to learn how much people prefer one thing over another, the
natural instinct is to ask them to rate each option on a scale: *"How
interesting does this class sound, on a scale of 1 to 10?"* The trouble
is that people use rating scales very differently. One student treats a 7
as faint praise; another treats a 7 as a rave. The numbers look
comparable but they aren't.

[**MaxDiff**]{.text-magenta}, also called *Best-Worst Scaling*, sidesteps
the problem by replacing absolute ratings with forced trade-offs. On
each screen the respondent sees a small subset of items — here four of
the ten core MSBA classes at UC San Diego Rady — and is asked to pick
the *most preferred* and the *least preferred* in that set. Humans are
much better at making side-by-side comparisons than at calibrating an
internal scale, so the resulting data carries a stronger signal about
true preference. (See the week-4 *MaxDiff* deck for a fuller treatment.)

The ten items in this study are the ten core classes in the Rady MSBA
program. The goal of the post is to estimate students' relative
preference for each class using three different methods and to see how
much they agree:

1. A simple [**counts analysis**]{.text-magenta} — for each class, the
   fraction of times it was picked best minus the fraction of times it
   was picked worst.
2. The [**multinomial logit (MNL)**]{.text-magenta} model fit by
   [**maximum likelihood**]{.text-magenta} (see week-5 conjoint/MNL deck
   for the derivation and the `optim` recipe — here we use `scipy`).
3. The same MNL model fit by [**Bayesian methods**]{.text-magenta} using
   a random-walk Metropolis–Hastings sampler (week-7 deck).

We expect all three methods to broadly agree on which classes are most
and least preferred. Where they differ is in how they quantify the
strength of preference and, more importantly, in how they communicate
uncertainty around the estimates.

## The Data

```{python}
#| label: load-data

choices = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_design_and_choices.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig")
labels  = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_item_labels.csv",
                      encoding="utf-8-sig",
                      usecols=["Item #", "Item"])
labels.columns = ["item", "label"]

# The survey contained two task types: 4-item MaxDiff screens (the focus
# of this assignment) and 2-item screens with a "none-of-these" option
# coded as item 11. We restrict to the 4-item MaxDiff tasks.
md = choices.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"]).filter(lambda g: len(g) == 4).copy()

N = md["Record ID"].nunique()
T_per_resp = int(md.groupby("Record ID")["Task"].nunique().iloc[0])
J = int(md.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"]).size().iloc[0])
n_items = int(md["Item"].nunique())
n_tasks = md.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"]).ngroups
```

```{python}
#| label: data-desc

desc = pd.DataFrame({

        "Respondents (N)",
        "MaxDiff tasks per respondent (T)",
        "Items shown per task (J)",
        "Total items in study",
        "Total MaxDiff observations (N × T)",
    ],
    "Value": [N, T_per_resp, J, n_items, n_tasks],
})
show(desc, caption="Study dimensions")
```

The dataset contains **`{python} N`** respondents, each of whom
completed **`{python} T_per_resp`** MaxDiff tasks of **`{python} J`**
items each, for a total of **`{python} n_tasks`** task observations
across the ten classes.

```{python}
#| label: sanity-check

# Every task should have exactly one +1, exactly one -1, and 2 zeros.
task_summ = (
    md.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"])["Response"]
      .agg(n_best=lambda x: (x == 1).sum(),
           n_worst=lambda x: (x == -1).sum(),
           n_zero=lambda x: (x == 0).sum())
)
sanity_ok = ((task_summ["n_best"] == 1) &
             (task_summ["n_worst"] == 1) &
             (task_summ["n_zero"] == 2)).all()
```

A sanity check confirms that **every task has exactly one *best*, one
*worst*, and two *neither* selections** — so the data is well-formed
(passed: `{python} sanity_ok`).

```{python}
#| label: exposure-counts

shown = (md.groupby("Item").size().rename("Times shown").reset_index()
           .rename(columns={"Item": "item"})
           .merge(labels, on="item")
           .sort_values("item")[["item", "label", "Times shown"]])
show(shown, caption="Number of times each class appeared across all tasks")
```

The MaxDiff design is balanced: every class was shown a similar number
of times across the study (272 appearances each), which is exactly what
we want so that the comparison across classes is fair.

## Counts Analysis

The simplest way to summarize MaxDiff data is to count picks. For each
item $j$, compute

$$
\text{score}_j \;=\; \%\text{best}_j \;-\; \%\text{worst}_j,
$$

where the percentages are taken out of the number of times the item was
*shown*. A score near $+1$ means a class is almost always picked best
when on screen; near $-1$ means almost always worst; near $0$ means it
is middle-of-the-pack or polarizing.

```{python}
#| label: counts-score

g = md.groupby("Item")["Response"]
best_n  = g.apply(lambda x: (x == 1).sum()).rename("best_n")
worst_n = g.apply(lambda x: (x == -1).sum()).rename("worst_n")
shown_n = g.size().rename("shown_n")

counts = pd.concat([shown_n, best_n, worst_n], axis=1).reset_index()
counts = counts.rename(columns={"Item": "item"}).merge(labels, on="item")
counts["pct_best"]  = counts["best_n"]  / counts["shown_n"]
counts["pct_worst"] = counts["worst_n"] / counts["shown_n"]
counts["score"]     = counts["pct_best"] - counts["pct_worst"]
counts = counts.sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

display_tbl = counts[["item", "label", "shown_n", "best_n", "worst_n",
                      "pct_best", "pct_worst", "score"]].rename(columns={
    "item": "Item", "label": "Class",
    "shown_n": "Shown", "best_n": "# Best", "worst_n": "# Worst",
    "pct_best": "% Best", "pct_worst": "% Worst", "score": "Score",
})
show(display_tbl,
     fmt={"% Best": "{:.1%}", "% Worst": "{:.1%}", "Score": "{:+.3f}"},
     caption="Counts analysis: classes ranked by (% best − % worst)")
```

```{python}
#| label: counts-bootstrap

# Bootstrap CI on the score by resampling respondents.
B = 1000
rid = md["Record ID"].unique()
boot_scores = np.zeros((B, n_items))
md_by_rid = {r: g for r, g in md.groupby("Record ID")}

for b in range(B):
    samp = np.random.choice(rid, size=len(rid), replace=True)
    pieces = [md_by_rid[r] for r in samp]
    bm = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True)
    bg = bm.groupby("Item")["Response"]
    sh = bg.size()
    bn = bg.apply(lambda x: (x == 1).sum())
    wn = bg.apply(lambda x: (x == -1).sum())
    sc = (bn / sh) - (wn / sh)
    boot_scores[b, sc.index.values - 1] = sc.values

lo = np.percentile(boot_scores, 2.5, axis=0)
hi = np.percentile(boot_scores, 97.5, axis=0)
counts["lo"] = counts["item"].map(lambda j: lo[j-1])
counts["hi"] = counts["item"].map(lambda j: hi[j-1])
```

```{python}
#| label: counts-plot
#| fig-cap: "Counts score (% best − % worst) by class, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from resampling respondents."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
y = np.arange(len(counts))[::-1]
ax.barh(y, counts["score"], color="#4C72B0", edgecolor="white")
err_lo = counts["score"] - counts["lo"]
err_hi = counts["hi"]    - counts["score"]
ax.errorbar(counts["score"], y, xerr=[err_lo, err_hi],
            fmt="none", ecolor="black", capsize=3, lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(counts["label"], fontsize=9)
ax.axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("% Best  −  % Worst")
ax.set_title("MaxDiff counts score per class (with 95% bootstrap CIs)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Even at the level of this simple count, the story is clear. **MGTA 495
Marketing Analytics** has by far the highest counts score: students pick
it as best far more often than they pick it as worst. **MGTA 455
Customer Analytics** and **MGTA 453 Business Analytics** are also
strongly liked. At the bottom, the **AI math/programming refresher
(MGTA 403)** and the **Analytics Consulting (MGTA 444)** course are
picked as *worst* much more often than as *best*. The 95% bootstrap
intervals on the top class do not overlap with anything in the middle
of the table, so its lead is statistically meaningful, not a sampling
fluke.

## From MaxDiff to MNL Choices

The counts analysis throws away information. It treats a "best" pick
the same regardless of *what it was competing against* on that screen
— picking a class as best from a strong set is harder than picking it
as best from a weak set. The multinomial logit (MNL) model fixes this
by modelling the choice process explicitly.

Assign each item $j$ a utility coefficient $\beta_j$. On a task showing
items $\{a, b, c, d\}$, the probability that item $b$ is picked *best*
is the soft-max,

$$
P(\text{best} = b) \;=\; \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}.
$$

The probability that item $c$ is then picked *worst* — from the
remaining three items with utilities *flipped* — is

$$
P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) \;=\; \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}.
$$

Each task therefore contributes [*two*]{.text-blue} MNL observations,
a best-pick from the full set and a worst-pick from the remaining set.

[**Identifiability.**]{.text-magenta} The soft-max is invariant to
adding a constant to every $\beta$, so only $J - 1 = 9$ of the ten
coefficients are identified separately. We fix $\beta_1 = 0$ (the AI
math course is the reference) and estimate $\beta_2, \dots, \beta_{10}$.
All preferences are read relative to this baseline.

```{python}
#| label: build-tasks

# For each task, store the 4 item ids, the best pick, and the worst pick.
tasks = []
for (_, _), g in md.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"], sort=False):
    items = g["Item"].to_numpy()
    resp  = g["Response"].to_numpy()
    tasks.append((items, int(items[resp == 1][0]), int(items[resp == -1][0])))

# Pre-stack as matrices for vectorized log-likelihood.
items_mat = np.stack([t[0] for t in tasks])         # (n_tasks, 4)
best_idx  = np.array([t[1] for t in tasks]) - 1     # (n_tasks,) zero-based
worst_idx = np.array([t[2] for t in tasks]) - 1
# For the "worst" softmax we need the 3 items remaining after dropping best
shown_idx = items_mat - 1                            # zero-based shown
mask_not_best = shown_idx != best_idx[:, None]       # True where item != best
```

## MNL via Maximum Likelihood

The full log-likelihood, summed over the `{python} n_tasks` tasks, is

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \;=\; \sum_{\text{tasks}} \Big[\, \beta_{j^*_b} \;-\; \log \!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown}}\!\!\! \exp(\beta_j) \;-\; \beta_{j^*_w} \;-\; \log \!\!\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}}\!\!\!\! \exp(-\beta_j) \,\Big],
$$

where $j^*_b$ and $j^*_w$ are the items picked best and worst on that
task. The log-sum-exp form keeps the numerics stable.

```{python}
#| label: mle

def neg_log_lik(beta_free):
    """beta_free has length 9; we pin beta_1 = 0."""
    beta = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_free])         # length 10
    v_shown = beta[shown_idx]                          # (n_tasks, 4)
    # Best-pick contribution
    ll_best = beta[best_idx] - logsumexp(v_shown, axis=1)
    # Worst-pick: drop the best from each row, use 3 remaining items
    n = shown_idx.shape[0]
    rem_idx = shown_idx[mask_not_best].reshape(n, 3)
    v_w     = -beta[rem_idx]
    ll_worst = -beta[worst_idx] - logsumexp(v_w, axis=1)
    return -(ll_best + ll_worst).sum()

x0  = np.zeros(9)
opt = minimize(neg_log_lik, x0, method="BFGS")
beta_mle = np.concatenate([[0.0], opt.x])

# Standard errors from the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood.
# scipy BFGS gives an approximate inverse Hessian (covariance) for the
# free params; build it back to a 10-vector by padding the reference.
cov_free = opt.hess_inv
se_free  = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_free))
se_mle   = np.concatenate([[0.0], se_free])

# Shares of preference: soft-max of the betas (sum to 1 across items).
shares_mle = np.exp(beta_mle) / np.exp(beta_mle).sum()

mle_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "item":   np.arange(1, 11),
    "beta":   beta_mle,
    "se":     se_mle,
    "share":  shares_mle,
}).merge(labels, on="item")
mle_tbl["rank"] = mle_tbl["share"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
mle_tbl = mle_tbl.sort_values("share", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

display_mle = mle_tbl[["rank", "item", "label", "beta", "se", "share"]].rename(columns={
    "rank": "Rank", "item": "Item", "label": "Class",
    "beta": "β̂", "se": "SE(β̂)", "share": "Share",
})
show(display_mle,
     fmt={"β̂": "{:+.3f}", "SE(β̂)": "{:.3f}", "Share": "{:.1%}"},
     caption="Maximum-likelihood estimates of the MNL coefficients and implied shares of preference. β₁ is pinned to 0 as the reference (MGTA 403).")
```

The standard errors come from the inverse of the negative Hessian
returned by `scipy.optimize.minimize`. To turn the raw $\hat\beta$'s
into something interpretable, we convert them to **shares of
preference** via the soft-max,

$$
\hat s_j \;=\; \frac{\exp(\hat\beta_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^{10} \exp(\hat\beta_k)},
$$

which sum to one and answer the natural question: *"if all ten classes
were on one screen, what fraction of best-picks would each one get?"*

```{python}
#| label: mle-plot
#| fig-cap: "MLE estimated share of preference for each class, sorted from highest to lowest."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
order = mle_tbl
y = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
ax.barh(y, order["share"], color="#55A868", edgecolor="white")
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(order["label"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated share of preference")
ax.set_title("MNL maximum-likelihood share of preference per class")
for yi, s in zip(y, order["share"]):
    ax.text(s + 0.003, yi, f"{s:.1%}", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0, order["share"].max() * 1.15)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The MNL ranking confirms what the counts already suggested: **MGTA 495
Marketing Analytics** dominates with an estimated share of about
**`{python} f"{mle_tbl.iloc[0]['share']:.0%}"`** of all best-picks if
the entire ten-class set were placed on a single screen. **MGTA 455
Customer Analytics** and **MGTA 453 Business Analytics** are clear
runners-up. The bottom three — **MGTA 444 Analytics Consulting**, the
**AI math/programming refresher**, and **MGTA 451 Marketing /
Finance / Operations** — sit well below the others. The order is
essentially identical to the counts ranking, which is reassuring: the
MNL is doing more work statistically, but on data this clean it lands
in the same place.

## MNL via Bayesian Estimation

The Bayesian recipe is the same likelihood, only now with a prior on
the coefficients:

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \;\propto\; L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$

A weakly informative prior $\boldsymbol{\beta} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\,
10 \cdot I)$ — a standard deviation of about $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ on
every coefficient — leaves the data to do almost all of the talking
while ruling out absurd values.

We sample from the posterior with a **random-walk Metropolis-Hastings
sampler**. Starting from the MLE, we propose
$\boldsymbol{\beta}^\ast = \boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$
with $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, s^2 I)$, accept with
probability $\min\{1, \, \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\ast)/\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})\}$,
and tune the step size $s$ to land at an acceptance rate of roughly
**25–40 %** (see the week-7 "Tuning the Step Size" slide).

```{python}
#| label: mcmc

PRIOR_VAR = 10.0

def log_lik(beta):
    v_shown = beta[shown_idx]
    ll_best = beta[best_idx] - logsumexp(v_shown, axis=1)
    n = shown_idx.shape[0]
    rem_idx = shown_idx[mask_not_best].reshape(n, 3)
    v_w     = -beta[rem_idx]
    ll_worst = -beta[worst_idx] - logsumexp(v_w, axis=1)
    return (ll_best + ll_worst).sum()

def log_prior(beta_free):
    return -0.5 * np.sum(beta_free ** 2) / PRIOR_VAR

def log_post(beta_free):
    beta = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_free])
    return log_lik(beta) + log_prior(beta_free)

def metropolis(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=495):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    K = len(beta0)
    draws = np.empty((n_iter, K))
    beta  = beta0.copy()
    lp    = log_post(beta)
    accept = 0
    for t in range(n_iter):
        prop  = beta + rng.normal(0.0, step, size=K)
        lp_p  = log_post(prop)
        if np.log(rng.random()) < (lp_p - lp):
            beta, lp = prop, lp_p
            accept  += 1
        draws[t] = beta
    return draws, accept / n_iter

n_iter = 30_000
burn   = n_iter // 4
draws, acc = metropolis(opt.x.copy(), n_iter=n_iter, step=0.10)
post = draws[burn:]

# Add the pinned beta_1 = 0 column.
post_full = np.concatenate([np.zeros((post.shape[0], 1)), post], axis=1)

beta_mean = post_full.mean(axis=0)
beta_sd   = post_full.std(axis=0)
beta_lo   = np.percentile(post_full, 2.5,  axis=0)
beta_hi   = np.percentile(post_full, 97.5, axis=0)

# Push every draw through the soft-max to get share posteriors.
exp_draws  = np.exp(post_full)
share_draws = exp_draws / exp_draws.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
share_mean = share_draws.mean(axis=0)
share_lo   = np.percentile(share_draws, 2.5,  axis=0)
share_hi   = np.percentile(share_draws, 97.5, axis=0)
```

The chain was run for **`{python} f"{n_iter:,}"`** iterations with a
step size of **0.10**, discarding the first
**`{python} f"{burn:,}"`** as burn-in. The acceptance rate was
**`{python} f"{acc*100:.1f}%"`**, comfortably inside the recommended
band.

```{python}
#| label: trace
#| fig-cap: "Trace plots for the post-burn-in MCMC chain on three representative coefficients. The 'fuzzy caterpillar' pattern indicates good mixing."

show_idx = [1, 4, 8]  # 0-based positions in the 9-dim free vector
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 7), sharex=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes, show_idx):
    ax.plot(post[:, k], lw=0.4, color="#4C72B0")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"β (item {k+2})")
    ax.set_xlim(0, len(post))
axes[-1].set_xlabel("post-burn-in iteration")
fig.suptitle("MCMC trace plots — random-walk Metropolis-Hastings")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The traces look like the canonical "fuzzy caterpillar": the chain is
moving around freely and revisiting the same range repeatedly, not
slowly drifting in one direction. That is what we want to see.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-table

bayes_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "item":        np.arange(1, 11),
    "beta_mean":   beta_mean,
    "beta_lo":     beta_lo,
    "beta_hi":     beta_hi,
    "share_mean":  share_mean,
    "share_lo":    share_lo,
    "share_hi":    share_hi,
}).merge(labels, on="item")
bayes_tbl["rank"] = bayes_tbl["share_mean"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
bayes_tbl = bayes_tbl.sort_values("share_mean", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

display_b = bayes_tbl[["rank", "item", "label",
                       "beta_mean", "beta_lo", "beta_hi",
                       "share_mean", "share_lo", "share_hi"]].rename(columns={
    "rank": "Rank", "item": "Item", "label": "Class",
    "beta_mean": "β̄",  "beta_lo": "β 2.5%", "beta_hi": "β 97.5%",
    "share_mean": "Share", "share_lo": "Share 2.5%", "share_hi": "Share 97.5%",
})
show(display_b,
     fmt={"β̄": "{:+.3f}", "β 2.5%": "{:+.3f}", "β 97.5%": "{:+.3f}",
          "Share": "{:.1%}", "Share 2.5%": "{:.1%}", "Share 97.5%": "{:.1%}"},
     caption="Posterior summaries for each class: posterior mean β, 95% credible interval on β, and the posterior of the implied share of preference.")
```

```{python}
#| label: bayes-plot
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean share of preference per class, with 95% credible intervals computed from the MCMC draws."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
order = bayes_tbl
y = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
ax.barh(y, order["share_mean"], color="#C44E52", edgecolor="white")
ax.errorbar(order["share_mean"], y,
            xerr=[order["share_mean"] - order["share_lo"],
                  order["share_hi"]   - order["share_mean"]],
            fmt="none", ecolor="black", capsize=3, lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(order["label"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Posterior mean share of preference")
ax.set_title("Bayesian MNL — posterior share of preference per class")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The Bayesian estimates land essentially on top of the MLEs: the
posterior mean of each $\beta$ is within a few hundredths of the MLE
point estimate, and the posterior standard deviations match the
classical standard errors. That is exactly what one should expect under
a diffuse prior and a large enough sample — the likelihood dominates the
posterior. What the Bayesian fit gives us *for free*, however, is a
proper credible interval on the **share of preference**: we just push
every MCMC draw through the soft-max and take quantiles. Obtaining the
same intervals from the MLE would require the delta method.

## Comparing the Three Methods

```{python}
#| label: comparison-table

cmp = (
    counts[["item", "label", "score"]]
      .rename(columns={"score": "Counts score"})
      .merge(mle_tbl[["item", "share", "rank"]]
                .rename(columns={"share": "MLE share", "rank": "MLE rank"}),
             on="item")
      .merge(bayes_tbl[["item", "share_mean", "rank"]]
                .rename(columns={"share_mean": "Bayes share",
                                 "rank": "Bayes rank"}),
             on="item")
)
cmp["Counts rank"] = cmp["Counts score"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
cmp = cmp[["item", "label",
           "Counts score", "Counts rank",
           "MLE share", "MLE rank",
           "Bayes share", "Bayes rank"]].sort_values("MLE rank")
cmp = cmp.rename(columns={"item": "Item", "label": "Class"})
show(cmp,
     fmt={"Counts score": "{:+.3f}",
          "MLE share": "{:.1%}", "Bayes share": "{:.1%}"},
     caption="All three methods side-by-side, sorted by MLE rank.")
```

```{python}
#| label: three-panel
#| fig-cap: "Side-by-side comparison of the three methods. Each panel sorts the ten classes by that method's score; bar colours are tied to the class so the same class can be traced across panels."

panel_df = cmp.copy()
panel_df = panel_df.merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")[
    ["Item", "Class", "Counts score", "MLE share", "Bayes share"]
]

cmap = plt.cm.tab10
colour_for_item = {i: cmap((i-1) % 10) for i in range(1, 11)}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 6))
for ax, (col, title, xlab) in zip(
    axes,
    [("Counts score", "Counts",   "% Best − % Worst"),
     ("MLE share",    "MLE",      "Share of preference"),
     ("Bayes share",  "Bayesian", "Posterior mean share")],
):
    o = panel_df.sort_values(col, ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
    y = np.arange(len(o))[::-1]
    cols = [colour_for_item[i] for i in o["Item"]]
    ax.barh(y, o[col], color=cols, edgecolor="white")
    ax.set_yticks(y)
    ax.set_yticklabels([lbl[:38] + ("…" if len(lbl) > 38 else "")
                        for lbl in o["Class"]], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlab)
    if col != "Counts score":
        ax.axvline(0.10, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
fig.suptitle("Three ways of ranking the ten MSBA classes", fontsize=13, y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The three methods agree completely on the top three and the bottom
three. Where they shuffle slightly is in the middle of the pack, where
classes have similar utilities and small amounts of sampling noise can
swap adjacent positions. This is exactly the regime in which the
Bayesian credible interval is most useful: it tells you which of the
middle-ranked classes are *meaningfully* different from one another and
which are essentially tied.

What does the MNL add over the counts analysis? The counts treat every
best-pick as equally informative, regardless of which items it competed
against. The MNL uses the full design — every item that was *shown but
not picked* also contributes information, because it was offered and
rejected. That extra information is what lets the model produce
interpretable shares of preference instead of just a bounded score.

What does the Bayesian fit add over the MLE? Two things. First, an
honest distribution over the *derived* quantities of interest. Shares
of preference, "what fraction of students would choose each class on a
single screen", or pairwise win probabilities are nonlinear functions
of the $\beta$'s, and quantifying their uncertainty from the MLE
requires the delta method or a parametric bootstrap. With MCMC every
draw gives you the derived quantity directly. Second, the framework
generalises gracefully — a hierarchical MNL with individual-level
coefficients is a small change to the same sampler and lets you measure
how preferences vary between students.

## Discussion

Reading these results as a prospective MSBA student rather than as a
modeller: **MGTA 495 Marketing Analytics** is the clear favourite among
the survey respondents. **MGTA 455 Customer Analytics** and **MGTA 453
Business Analytics** form a strong second tier. The **Capstone** and
**SQL** classes sit in the middle — useful courses that no one rates as
their absolute favourite but that few rate as their least favourite
either. At the bottom are the **AI math/programming refresher** and the
**Analytics Consulting** course, both picked as worst much more often
than as best.

A methodological summary in three lines:

* The **counts analysis** is the right tool for an executive dashboard
  — it is transparent, requires no model, and lands on the same broad
  ranking that the more sophisticated methods produce.
* **Maximum-likelihood MNL** gives the same ranking but adds principled
  standard errors and lets you compute shares of preference. It is the
  default workhorse when you want a single number to report with a
  classical error bar.
* **Bayesian MNL** wins when you need uncertainty on *derived*
  quantities (shares, market simulations, "what if we added an
  eleventh class?" scenarios) or when you want to extend the model
  hierarchically to estimate preferences at the *individual* level
  rather than only on average.

A few caveats are worth flagging. The respondents are a self-selected
sample of MSBA students — preferences here may not generalise to other
analytics programs, or even to future cohorts at Rady. Each respondent
saw eight tasks of four items, which gives a clean *aggregate* picture
but is too thin to estimate stable preferences for any individual
student. Finally, students' preferences are partly shaped by their
prior coursework and by where they currently are in the program — an
obvious next step would be to fit a hierarchical MNL with a
student-level effect, or to interact the $\beta$'s with covariates such
as concentration or work experience to see whether different segments
of students prefer different sets of classes.
